This is October 6, 1981 at the Institute of Jazz Studies. My name is Ron Welburn, and I'm interviewing Teddy McRae for the Jazz Oral History Project. Teddy, welcome to the Institute.
Thank you.

And thank you for participating in the Oral History Project. Teddy, I wonder if you would start out from the beginning -- if you could give us your full name and spell your last name. And tell us where you were born and something about your family.

Well, my full name was not my stage -- I'll say this. My name is Theodore McRae, "M-c-R-a-e. My stage name is Teddy, T-e-d-d-y M-c-R-a-e. Is that capital R? Capital R, yes. I was born in Philadelphia in 1908. My family is from Atlanta. They moved some time ago, and I was practically raised in Philly, and since I had six
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

other brothers and one sister. She was the baby sister. My oldest brother was named William McRae. My second oldest brother was named Floyd McRae. Dave McRae is my third oldest brother. I came after Dave, then Bob McRae who was called Robert McRae, was my youngest brother. My sister was in-between myself and Bob, the youngest one -- youngest brother. We raised in Philly, went to school there. My father was -- moved from Atlanta early in life, and he worked around Philly as a real estate man. We own quite a lot of property around Philly.
In the city itself or outside?

In the city itself. Early on -- in the early life, my oldest brother was into the music business. He was a very fine pianist. And I guess that's where we got our education -- you know, experience from him, (inaudible) get into the music business. He taught us all, (inaudible) down the
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
line -- Bob, you know, from one to the other. My oldest brother was William McRae and Floyd McRae. They were the first to (inaudible). They were playing around Philly clubs, like that.
You remember any of the clubs that they played?
Well, no. Just like little small clubs, (inaudible) gigging around Philly.

My oldest brother was like -- he would study. He was (inaudible) like a concert pianist, and he worked a couple of movie houses back in those days, I want to say. They didn't have, you know, the silent movies, and he used to play the Earl Theater on South Street. we used to go (inaudible) watch him play the piano -- play all these -- you know, one time western and country. Story of the cowboys, story of -- (inaudible). Comedy things, yes.
Comedy things (inaudible) just playing the piano and all that kind of stuff.
Keystone Cops and that sort of thing.
Yes. But on the weekend,
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

he would have like -- outstanding piano players would come down from Philly, (inaudible). My mother had a second floor which was really a sun parlor. And in that room my father had bought him two baby grand pianos and it was locked together. And he'd have these different piano players come in (inaudible), like Paul Lamoar, from Baltimore, Washington -- like come down on the weekend and visit us.
Do you remember -- I know you were small boy then -- but do you remember any names?

No, I don't. I can't remember any of the names. I always wondered who these fellows were. I know they used to come like on the weekend for a visit. And like on a Saturday morning they'd have tea or coffee and they'd go up in the room and they'd close the door. And then you wouldn't hear anything for about ten or fifteen minutes. Then they would start off.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

They wouldn't come out. They wouldn't I'd know let me in there -- I was little -- because (inaudible) what they were doing. And they would be going over these different classic piano concerto things. They'd be doing that on the weekend.

I couldn't remember. That used to bug me a lot. I always wanted to know who some of those people were, but I didn't bother about it because eventually when I got into high school, I got into the band -- played in the high school band.
I bought my own saxophone. See, I used to work after school in the drug store with Dr. Miller at North Philadelphia (inaudible) 22nd and Susquehanna (inaudible) Avenue, something like that.
And coming home from school one day, I passed the pawn shop. And I saw this beautiful horn in the window. I said, 'Oh, that's for me. I like that.'

Why I got interested in tenor, Paul Whiteman came to Philadelphia one year. My brother took me to see Paul Whiteman and his big band. this boy came down to the mike and And (inaudible) played this beautiful
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
tenor -- beautiful solo. That's the instrument I wanted to play from then on. I said I wanted to buy me a tenor sax. And I worked and bought my own saxophone.
You hadn't fooled around with a saxophone before?
No, I hadn't fooled around with a saxophone.
You just saw it in the window.
I just saw it in the window, and (inaudible). That was years ago. And I'm goin to buy me a saxophone. I said, (inaudible).
You lived in North Philadelphia near 22nd and Susquehanna (inaudible) Avenue?

Yes, 22nd and Diamond. We lived at 22nd and Diamond. We were the very -- very exclusive That was a (inaudible) neighborhood by my father being a real estate man. He bought in that neighborhood. And then he died earlier in my life. I think I was about 15 years old when he passed away.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
And my mother raised us. She took over the problems. Then we moved back to South Philly.

And we went to school in Philly -- all my brothers. I think my sister, Bob and I, we studied mostly in Philly. But my two oldest brothers before they came they were in college, in Morehouse (inaudible), and things like that.
What high school did you go to? was in South were you (inaudible) Philadelphia?
North Philly.
Gratz or -- there's Simn (inaudible) there's gratz up there, at Northeast High?
I think it was Northeast.
That's now called Thomas Edison --
Yeah, Thomas Edison.
Northeast High School. Did you play in any school bands or orchestras?
I played in the school band. Like I said before, when I -- I studied a lot. I studied off a fellow named Mike Gunable, a very
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

fine teacher. A very fine teacher. He was very fine. And I studied with him for quite a while. I forgotten how many years I studied with him.. It was during the time I was going to school. And we used to study on a Sunday and maybe twice a week. He was very strict. He gave you to do after you came in. things (inaudible) And he turned me out. (Inaudible) became a very outstanding tenor player, but I didn't play much around Philly when I was kid. I was young, in my 20's or something like that. I didn't play much around Philly. I had an offer to come to Atlantic City to play in one of the clubs there. And that's where I met Claude Hopkins. And he had a little small band there. And I heard Hilton Jefferson and Elmore Williams, the tenor player that wind up with Chick. But that was way before. There were those two guys, the finest tenor players that anybody wanted to listen to. They had (inaudible) a saxophone team --
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

Claude Hopkins band -- it's a little club down there. I ran across -- there's been a lot of good musicians in Philly at that time -- in Atlantic City at that time. There was the Egg Harbor Club there with a great band in it, and there was Charlie Taylor, the colored violinist -- they had a great band out at Egg Harbor. Big band there. And you had a chance to really here -- as young as I was, I heard some great musicians down there in Atlantic City. Then I have to go back home -- go back to school, you know.
You were still in high school at this time.
Yeah.
I see. So, the Claude Hopkins Band was shortly after he returned from overseas.
Yeah. He had a fine band. A little small band. It wasn't too big. It was like two saxophones, rhythm, and maybe a trumpet. Most of those bands had banjos, and I
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
don't think -- I think he did have a banjo in that band. Didn't have no guitar. They used to have banjos.
Do you remember some of the other people who were in that band?
No. (Inaudible). I know it's in one of my books. I'd have to lok that up.
Who were some of your musical compatriots in Philadelphia who may be known by the jazz public as well as relatively unknown? People who you may have played with or studied with?
Well, the fellow I just -- I don't know if anybody know this fellow's name, Mike Gunable. He was one of the top teachers in the East.
And really, though, I think he came from St. Louis. Somebody recommended me to him as a teacher. And he really turned me out. He was really a fine teacher.
He give you things to do. He'll tell you to come to practice on a Sunday, and leave your horn -- don't bring your horn. Just bring your
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
mouthpiece.

And this way, he would strengthen up your muscles and your -- you know, the lower part of your neck so you don't move your mouthpiece around when you're playing. You don't stick your jaw out, you don't develop a lot of wind. It developes the muscles so your face will look the same way when you're blowing.
In other words, you had your --

Yeah, just hold your mouthpiece and just blow in it. That would develop your tone. This was very important. This was one of the things that I think that gave me the tone and technique (inaudible) I had -- I was recommended for that.
Everybody thought I had a beautiful tone and my technique. So --
You were playing a tenor at that time.
Yeah. Tenor and then he put me on clarinet.
What model?
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
I was playing -- that was a King horn. Remember that big bell that King used to have. That was a King horn.
No, no, not a King. What was that, you'd mentioned a King to me. It wasn't a King.
Conn.
They were very popular in the (inaudible).
Yeah. Well King was too. Because most of your band instruments were King. Must remember mostly all the schools and colleges bought King instruments.
How about the Bueschers?
Well it was popular, it was good. But it wasn't as popular as some of the King horns.
King was most of the big bands, the great big silver bass, and things like that -- was a King horn.
But the Conn was the most thing you'd buy -- dance bands and things. And Conn made a lot of band stuff too. They were very popular.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Until -- I forget the year that Selmer came in. I think Selmer came in in '38 was when it hit this country.
Because '37 when Coleman Hawkins was in Europe, they tell me he was blowing a Selmer horn, we was asking, 'What's that horn that Coleman Hawkins use?' And that was Selmer.
I see.
Okay. Gunable also had you do some work on clarinet.
Yeah, he taught me. He had to -- see, he always said that you have to learn the clarinet because the clarinet will make you a much better saxophone player. Because clarinet was hard, you know.

And the clarinet was a very necessary instrument for any reed man. (inaudible). Eventually will have to learn the clarinet, so you might as well get on it at an early stage where you can take it along with you. With the saxophone, you know.
Because the clarinet is an instrument -- that would be your natural double, you know. Come out

to be your double. The double on the flute didn't come till later and I never did get to (inaudible) the flute. I went to the bass clarinet. My double was bass. Was a E-flat (inaudible) soprano, bass clarinet, tenor, bass sax and alto. When we -- my brother built his band and decided when they were working around Philly, decided that -- he got together with a lot of musicians out of Baltimore. At that time in the early 20's, '28 it was a lot of good musicians around Philly. And Baltimore was turning out some good brass men. My brother got together with these fellows and they put this band together. And he asked me did I want to come down to Atlantic City and join the band. So, my brother -- Bill and Floyd and myself. We was the three brothers in the McRae Brothers Band at that time when we put this band together. It was Bill and Floyd --
What were they playing?
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
My oldest brother, Bill -- William McRae, he played piano and arranged. My second oldest brother, Floyd McRae, now, he was a tremendous alto player.
It was Rudy Wiedoft played with Paul Whiteman who's one of the finest alto players in the country...
And these two guys supposed to be the best. My brother was supposed to be rared along with him. And he was tremendous alto player.
And we set up this band -- we went to Atlantic City and we stayed there a year. They built a club called the "Old Rhine."
Old Rhine?
They named it like O --
O'Ryan, I see. O apostrophe R-y-a-n.
Yes. They wanted to call it the McRae Brothers, but they didn't call it that. They just called it something -- (inaudible) they built it -- "we're going to name the club after yall, you know."
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
And we had this beautiful band. First time they had four saxophones in there. We went in there with four saxophones.
Who were the other two saxophone players?
Oh boy. It's been so long. See, the only thing about that band -- see, it's very hard to remember who those fellows were, because you understand, we only had this band together for one summer.
The whole time I was there, I -- we used to work in a night club and it'll be all night long. And we get off like five or six o'clock in the morning.
I'd just stay 'round the club and practice a little bit.
You started around nine at night?
'Round nine --
So it was a nine to five gig --
The first show was ten.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

Yeah, it was a long gig. Because we always had a breakfast dance. You know, a breakfast show. Something like Sunday mornings we get off at six o'clock in the morning -- seven o'clock because you had that breakfast show start at five. I'd stay in the club and practice on my bass. Everybody will be gone and I'd stay in the club and practice, practice, practice, you know. Then I'd go home and get some sleep, like that.
You also had a little training on piano that your older brother helped you with, or did you --

No, I didn't bother the piano. I really didn't bother too much with the piano. Just a little bit I could play it, but I didn't bother with the piano at all. After we put this band together, we went there -- we moved into New York. That was on the 29th. I think that was 1929 when we came to
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
New York, that winter --
Okay.

The fall of '29. I think the summer of '29 when we played Atlantic City. That was the summer of '29 -- 1929. We came into New York of the winter of -- like September. You know, after Atlantic City closed we came into New York with the band. We played 129th Street. It was a private club -- Barron's. Was a 129th Street and Lenox downstairs there was a club. It was a private club. It was put up by these real estate fellows. They had released it out to just people at formal dances and things. We played like four or five days there -- it was night. Then we played at -- There was another place we were doing. We were broadcasting over -- Nola I know a studio had a broad -- I think it was NBC or CBS up there on the top floor, 111 (inaudible) 57th Street -- Nola know it was a studio up there.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
But that was a big studio broadcasting. We worked there every night. We used to broadcast every night from 5:30 to 6.
And we were broadcasting everyday there. You know, like supper music -- what you call supper music.
And we had this beautiful band --
The McRae Brothers.
Yeah, McRae Brothers.
And we were broadcasting and people didn't know -- they really didn't know -- they only heard the band --
They probably didn't know it was a colored band or a white band, because the band was smooth pretty band with all the saxophones.
We used to have like E-flat soprano, B-flat soprano, C melody, and a clarinet. We give you the sound of real high voices. Real pretty high voices.
And we would start off like that and then we would go -- gradually go down to the four saxophones and come back to the clarinet and the muted
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

brass. And people thought that this was a band from out West, you know. And when we went to the Savoy, we played -- They invited us to the Savoy one Sunday to paly against Fess William. And everybody was astonished to find out that this band was a colored band and had been in town for about a month playing over at a radio station, and they never had seen a picture or anything, you know. And Fess Williams himself didn't know how good this band was. He was up there with his clarinet. You know, you ever see Fess Williams' clarinet with all the rhinestones and things in it -- the hat with the rhinestones. He was just jumping up and down and his band was just playing. And we came out and we set up on the other bandstand. And when we hit -- I never could see the expression on his face, because he never expected a band like that. We had this fellow, a real tall fellow (inaudible)
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

play the bass horn. At that time, he played like, pedaling bass -- had a thing that rolled. It wasn't the type of bass that you had the Four (inaudible) things that you had to push down. They had a thing like the pedal. Like it was rolling.
His notes came out like an organ. When the band would be playing something, he'd just be rolling -- the bass would be just be rolling just like an organ, you know -- bass like that.
And they never heard anything like that. And we'd go in these fast things, you know.
What was his name? Do you recall?
Do you recall some of the other band members in the McRae Brothers Band?
No. I'd have to get them for you later on. I'm really going to look that up and find out who was in that band.
I have to call my brother on the coast and find out for you who played, because he's in California now. Out in Oakland, California.
Who played the C melody
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
My brother did. Floyd played the C melody.
What do you think of that instrument?
Well, that is one of the finest instruments. I don't know why they don't use it more often.

I really couldn't understand the bands today as to why they never used it. Now they used everything -- Now you can understand -- we had -- Guess what we had? We had a bass saxophone, tenor -- that's what I played, tenor -- soprano, and bass clarinet. It was an instrument I played -- just a horn. Now here my brother over there, he's playing C melody, clarinet, E-flat soprano, you know. The other guy playing baritone and clarinet and alto. And all of them are doubling on two or three instruments, you know. And we came in with all those instruments.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
And people say, 'Gee, what...?' When I went on the road with Chick -- eventually I joined Chick later -- I went on the road with all these instruments.
My bass clarinet, bass sax, soprano, clarinet, you know, and tenor. They say, 'Gee, this guy is a whole music store. When is he going to get through setting up all these instruments?'

Well everybody in the band played -- the flute had came in then. We had a couple of the guys in the band who played flute, clarinet, soprano. With Chick Webb (inaudible), I think we had four sopranos. Four sopranos are beautiful when you hear them all together.
Or, either three sopranos -- E-flat sopranos. E-flat soprano, alto and two sopranos give you a whole new sound -- whole new thing. A whole new sound.
Gives you like voices like. Like, you know, just something that --
Right today, I haven't seen a band yet that played (inaudible). I ran across a band in

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Detroit when we're playing with Chick. The guy had an E-flat soprano. And it's beautiful. It's a wonderful saxophone, but nobody played it.
Few people play it anymore.
[Pharoah]
I think Ferrell, Sanders --
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
Had played it once in a while.
When we were in Atlantic City, Coon-Sanders was there -- the band from out west.
(Inaudible) Coon Sanders and Black Hawks.
Yeah, the Black Hawks. Now the fellow that played bass sax -- I forget his name, he's very popular.
Rollini?
Yeah. See, Rollini and he --
I got my inspiration from him from playing bass saxophone. They did a thing called
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
"Stomping the Dog and Kicking The Cat." And this was something that the bass saxophone played. They featured a bass saxophone on this. And I got one.
Then Coleman Hawkins with Fletcher back in those days -- and Coleman played bass. Coleman was a great bass saxophone player! I think he was just as good as Rollini or any of the guys.
When I came to New York, I said I got to hear Coleman play that bass saxophone.
Coleman had a -- Chick finally got this arrangement from Fletcher for me. It was a thing -- I forget the name of it. I was all for bass saxophone.
And then, (inaudible) that's the thing, Chick used to feature me on bass saxophone. And then he used to feature me on "By-Heck."
"By-Heck."
You know, with the breaks in it? Instead of him making the drum break, he let me make the breaks. I make some of the breaks and he makes some of the breaks. And they came out real good.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Well, it leads me to ask if at that time some of the writers for the orchestra when the saxophone section reached three men and four players.
It was a lot of writing for those sections. Sometimes you'd have a trio, as you say, with a kind of different instrumentation, or with the use of a bass sax.
Is that something that happened occasionally, or is it...?
Oh no. You mean like writing for those instruments backing us? No. That was a --
Special thing.

Special things we used to do. And just remember that most are like -- take for instance my brother, Bill, the oldest one, he was an excellent pianist. And not only an excellent (inaudible) pianist, but he's an excellent writer. He can arrange.
So he's the one that wrote for the McRae Brothers Band.

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Yeah. He's an excellent arranger. Plus, we had other trumpet players in the band who could write.

Most of the musicians back there, they learned arranging also. They used to write -- the players would learn how to arrange -- they were good trumpet players -- they would study arranging and things like that.
And we had a lot of arrangements back in those days.
And then, here's something that went on with bands that you probably wouldn't...

We used to sit down and put things together. Like, head (inaudible) arrangements. And sometimes your head (inaudible) arrangement would turn our better than anything in the book was written in the book, because this would be something for everybody.
Each member would -- like you say, "Well, we'll do this. You play this, we'll play this. We'll put a background to this melody here. And when you do something, we'll put a background to
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

what you're doing." Then the trombones -- maybe we got trombones -- they'll be doing something. And the bass will say, "I'll play this in here. I'll do this beat here and that'll make it do so and so and so."
Teddy, let's back up a bit.
Okay. Let's go back to uh...
You studied medicine. Tell us a little about that. Where did you study?

Yes. When I was working in the drug store with Dr. Miller, he thought that I could have -- he was interested in me going into medicine. "Come on, why don't you be a doctor? What you wanna mess with music for?" I said, "Well, you know, I don't think my mother has that kind of money. It takes a lot of money to be a doctor." He said, "Oh no." He had a position
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
in the hospital. He owned the drug store, but he was also in -- I forget the name of the hospital. I think it was Hoffman Hospital. A big hospital in Philly like the medical center here.
Hoffman?
Uh...
Hahnemann Hospital.
Yeah, Hahnemann Hospital.
He was there.
I see.
He really wanted me to -- I was working for him, you know, for two or three years. You know, while I was going through high school.
He was really interested in me studying medicine. By working around the drug store, you learn a lot of things.
And he thought maybe -- you know, "This guy, he catches on. Why don't you go into medicine?"
I said, "I just started playing music," like that. I said, "I don't think my mother has the money to really put me through medicine." I said, "I
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

don't think so."
So he said, "Well look, study with me for a while."
So he send me -- you know, went down to the school -- went down to the hospital and work out from there.
But I worked with him for about a year. That's when I first went to Atlantic City with my brothers and I didn't get back -- I didn't come back to it anymore.
But after that -- see, when we moved -- when we came to New York, that was it, you know.
But off and on with Dr. Miller, the whole time I was with him, he was interested in me studying medicine.
I did study, you know. Started to really get into it, but the money wasn't there.
You know, it was something my brother was pushing me to do with them, because my two oldest brothers, they had this band thing out here going.
And they found out I was staying,
(Inaudible) I came out so good. They said, "Look, we'll take Ted and we'll put him in the

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
band, and then it'll be the three of us. We'll call it the McRae Brothers Band. Come on, we're going to Atlantic City. We're going to do this."
And they had their own ideas. I say, "Okay, I'm with you guys."
Then we came to New York, and that's when we got into (inaudible).
Before you went to New York, you were with June Clark.
No. This is when we came into New York.
After leaving Atlantic City, we came -- like I told you, we worked at this club and we also broadcast.
But we worked around New York -- I think just before Thanksgiving. This band didn't stay -- we came in around -- we closed after Labor Day in Atlantic City.
You weren't quite 20 at this time. I guess you were out of high school by this time.
Yeah, yeah. I was out --

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
This would be about 1927.

Yeah. So, when we came to New York -- We came to New York around '29. It was the year '29. 1929 when we came to New York. Because we played Atlantic City the summer of '29, see. We came into New York and we played -- we did the broadcasts and we played -- did some gigs at the Savoy one night up here. And we worked at this club, 129th Street. That's where we stayed there. And the club closed.
Is that the Club Ebony?

Yeah, Club Ebony. We closed there I think like Thanksgiving Eve, or something. After that, Thanksgiving Day we were off. Because I know we were standing on the corner and one of my brothers said some of the guys wanted to go back to Baltimore, some of them want to
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
go back to Philly. My brother says, 'Well, I'll tell you what we're going to do. Let's go to Buffalo.' Now he knew some people -- (End of Tape 1 Side A) So he broke the --
(Inaudible).

Yeah, let's go to Buffalo. He wanted to go to Buffalo. I said, 'I don't want to go to Buffalo.' 'Maybe I'll stay around New York for a while.' So, my two oldest brothers, Bill and Floyd, they went to Buffalo. Now they worked around Buffalo -- they had their own little combos around there -- they worked around Buffalo for a long while. They stayed in Buffalo for quite a while. And I stayed in New York. And this is when I met June Clark. He was playing down at a dance -- 14th Street -- a little
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
dancing school. It was very popular, those dancing schools.
You'd come in and buy tickets to dance with the girls, and things like that.
Were those called "dime dances or nickel dances?"
Yeah, dime dances. Yeah, where the guy come in and buy a roll of tickets and dance with the girl two or three dances.
We worked there. June had this -- it was a good band. A real good band, played good music.

You had to play waltzes and everything -- you know, fox trots and everything. And it was a good learning thing, because you got a chance to really learn all the music -- the different styles and things you never even played.
It really was a breaking out point. And I've never forget when we got Lawrence (inaudible) -- I was with him for about six months and we needed a guitar and we brought in Lawrence Lucie.
And Lawrence Lucie was just begin to --

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: Opening of the interview, October 1981
segments.summary: Welburn introduces the Jazz Oral History Project interview with Teddy McRae at the Institute of Jazz Studies and asks him to begin with his background.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: Born in Philadelphia; the McRae family and brothers
segments.summary: McRae gives his name, says he was born in Philadelphia in 1908, and names his brothers and sister; his father was a real estate man.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: Oldest brother William, pianist at the movie house
segments.summary: His eldest brother was a fine pianist who taught the others, and played silent films at the Earl Theater on South Street while William and Floyd gigged in small clubs.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: Visiting pianists and the two baby grands
segments.summary: Pianists from Baltimore and Washington came on weekends to play classical pieces on the two baby grands his father bought for the sun parlor.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: High school band, buying a tenor saxophone
segments.summary: McRae joins the high school band, works in Dr. Miller's drugstore, buys a saxophone from a pawnshop after hearing a tenor solo with Paul Whiteman.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: Neighborhood at 22nd and Diamond; father's death
segments.summary: The family lived in an exclusive North Philadelphia neighborhood; his father died when he was about fifteen and his mother raised the children.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: Studying with Mike Gunable; first trip to Atlantic City
segments.summary: McRae studied with a strict teacher, Mike Gunable, then got an offer in Atlantic City where he met Claude Hopkins and heard Hilton Jefferson and Elmer Williams.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: Atlantic City musicians: Egg Harbor Club, Claude Hopkins's small band
segments.summary: He recalls the good musicians in Atlantic City, Charlie Taylor's band at the Egg Harbor Club, and the small instrumentation of the Hopkins band.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: Gunable's mouthpiece exercises for tone
segments.summary: Gunable, a top East Coast teacher, had pupils build embouchure strength by blowing the mouthpiece alone, which McRae credits for his tone.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: King, Conn, Buescher and Selmer saxophones
segments.summary: Welburn and McRae sort out which horn he played and discuss the popularity of King, Conn and Buescher, and the arrival of Selmer in 1938.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: Learning clarinet as a double
segments.summary: Gunable insisted on clarinet, which McRae calls the natural double for any reed man; his own doubles were bass clarinet and bass sax.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: Forming the McRae Brothers Band
segments.summary: His brothers recruit Baltimore musicians for a band and invite him to Atlantic City; William arranged and played piano, Floyd played alto.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: Playing the O'Ryan club in Atlantic City
segments.summary: The band played a new club with four saxophones, working nine to five with a breakfast show; McRae practiced bass in the empty club.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: Moving the band to New York; Barron's and radio broadcasts
segments.summary: After Atlantic City the band came to New York, played Barron's on 129th Street and did supper-music broadcasts that listeners took for a white band.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: Savoy Ballroom contest against Fess Williams
segments.summary: Invited to the Savoy to play against Fess Williams, the band surprised the audience, who had not known it was Black; the bassist played a pedal-type bass.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: Saxophone voicings: C melody, E-flat soprano, bass clarinet
segments.summary: Floyd played C melody; McRae praises the instrument and describes the doubling and the unusual saxophone sound of the band.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: E-flat soprano, Coon-Sanders, and Rollini as bass sax inspiration
segments.summary: McRae recalls hearing an E-flat soprano in Detroit with Chick, and Adrian Rollini's bass sax with Coon-Sanders as his inspiration.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: Chick Webb features bass sax and "By-Heck"
segments.summary: Coleman Hawkins also played bass sax; Chick Webb got McRae a Henderson arrangement and let him trade breaks on "By-Heck".

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: Arranging and head arrangements in the McRae band
segments.summary: William wrote for the band; sidemen learned arranging, and head arrangements worked out collectively often beat written ones.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: Dr. Miller urges him to study medicine
segments.summary: The Philadelphia druggist, who held a post at Hahnemann Hospital, pushed McRae toward medicine, but money was short and the band took him to Atlantic City.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
segments.title: McRae Brothers close at Club Ebony; brothers leave for Buffalo
segments.summary: McRae dates the band's New York stay to 1929; after the Club Ebony closed at Thanksgiving, Bill and Floyd went to Buffalo and he stayed in New York.

segments.chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
segments.title: Joining June Clark's band at the 14th Street dancing school
segments.summary: Left in New York, McRae met trumpeter June Clark and joined his band at a dime-a-dance school, where he taught guitarist Lawrence Lucie the ropes.

segments.chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
segments.title: Where the 14th Street dancing school stood
segments.summary: They pin the school down near 14th Street and Irving Place, next to a theater by Union Square.

segments.chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
segments.title: How the dime dances worked
segments.summary: Men bought tickets to dance with hostesses; classes ran by day to records and the band played evenings, with a clean, well-run atmosphere.

segments.chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
segments.title: Playing pop tunes and waltzes for the dancers
segments.summary: Songs had to be kept short; the band played all the popular music, show tunes and waltzes, which made the schools a good training ground.

segments.chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
segments.title: The Rhythm Club as a place to cut and learn
segments.summary: McRae contrasts today's young players with the Rhythm Club on 132nd and 7th, where top musicians cut each other and Hawkins, Waller and Hines came by.

segments.chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
segments.title: Union scale and pay in the dance school
segments.summary: The dancing schools drew few name musicians; McRae says fifty dollars a week was good money, with union scale around fifty-five at Chick Webb's.

segments.chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
segments.title: Living in Harlem; his wife Freddi
segments.summary: McRae rented the first floor of a private house on 137th Street and sent for his wife, a fellow church member, and they married in New York.

segments.chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
segments.title: June Clark's band at the Club Kentucky
segments.summary: After the dancing school the band followed Duke Ellington into the mob-run Club Kentucky at 49th and Broadway, where the gangsters treated musicians well.

segments.chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
segments.title: June Clark, trumpeter who lost his upper register
segments.summary: McRae calls Clark one of the outstanding 1930s trumpeters, once rated with Armstrong, until a split lip left him unable to play high.

segments.chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
segments.title: The dancing school as a learning ground
segments.summary: Playing under Clark, a learned musician, let McRae put his teacher's lessons to work and learn a range of styles.

segments.chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
segments.title: Hired by Charlie Johnson after the McRae Brothers
segments.summary: Charlie Johnson heard the McRae Brothers in Atlantic City and called McRae back to New York in January 1929, after a missed meeting at the station.

segments.chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
segments.title: With Charlie Johnson at Ed Small's club and Small's Paradise
segments.summary: McRae worked about a couple of months at Small's 5th Avenue club, then about a year at Small's Paradise, where he met Benny Waters and Benny Carter.

segments.chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
segments.title: Charlie Johnson's band, its arrangers, and its 1927 recordings
segments.summary: Welburn reads off the sidemen on the Charlie Johnson RCA reissue, including Jabbo Smith, Sidney De Paris and Monette Moore, as McRae comments.

segments.chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
segments.title: Ben Whitted, lead alto with Charlie Johnson
segments.summary: McRae remembers the Hampton-schooled altoist Ben Whitted as a gentleman, pipe-smoking and clean living, who walked home with him and Benny Waters.

segments.chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
segments.title: Bobby Johnson, Jimmy Harrison and the Johnson drummer
segments.summary: The two discuss Bobby Johnson on banjo, Jimmy Harrison on trombone and the drummer, George Stafford, a sharp dresser.

segments.chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
segments.title: How McRae moved between Johnson's Atlantic City and New York jobs
segments.summary: He played with Johnson in Atlantic City for a summer and returned to Small's Paradise for the winter in New York.

segments.chapter: Harlem and Atlantic City nightlife
segments.title: The flapper age and Harlem as playground of the world
segments.summary: McRae says the 1920s were great: the charleston, the radio, and Harlem as the showplace where everybody came, from the Savoy to Connie's Inn.

segments.chapter: Harlem and Atlantic City nightlife
segments.title: The Cotton Club and Small's Paradise, top clubs
segments.summary: The Cotton Club and Small's Paradise were the top clubs; Charlie Johnson produced most of the Small's shows with singers like Mattie Hite.

segments.chapter: Harlem and Atlantic City nightlife
segments.title: Cover charges at the Cotton Club and today's pay
segments.summary: A night at the Cotton Club cost five to seven dollars; McRae compares those days with groups who now earn too much too fast.

segments.chapter: Harlem and Atlantic City nightlife
segments.title: Bouncers at Small's Paradise, Connie's Inn and the Savoy
segments.summary: The big clubs were protected by strong-arm men, some ex-prizefighters, who kept the crowds in line and quietly removed troublemakers.

segments.chapter: Harlem and Atlantic City nightlife
segments.title: End of Tape 1 and start of Tape 2
segments.summary: Welburn closes the first tape, then opens Tape 2 of the interview.

segments.chapter: Harlem and Atlantic City nightlife
segments.title: Philadelphia clubs compared with New York and Atlantic City
segments.summary: McRae says Philadelphia had a few hotels and clubs but no real excitement, unlike New York or Atlantic City.

segments.chapter: Harlem and Atlantic City nightlife
segments.title: Atlantic City's clubs, Million Dollar Pier and boardwalk
segments.summary: Atlantic City had the Million Dollar Pier, the Silver Slipper, Paradise and many clubs, whose bills were much richer than today's one-star shows.

segments.chapter: Harlem and Atlantic City nightlife
segments.title: Camden and southern New Jersey
segments.summary: Camden had little to offer a big band; trains ran straight to Atlantic City.

segments.chapter: Depression gigs, Lil Armstrong, joining Chick Webb
segments.title: End of the McRae Brothers Band
segments.summary: McRae explains that the band was put together for Atlantic City, broadcast in New York, and ended in 1929 when Bill and Floyd left for Buffalo.

segments.chapter: Depression gigs, Lil Armstrong, joining Chick Webb
segments.title: Depression years and the Rhythm Club as hiring hall
segments.summary: McRae and Chick Webb scuffled in the Depression, and the Rhythm Club was where musicians waited for calls and the union sent bands out.

segments.chapter: Depression gigs, Lil Armstrong, joining Chick Webb
segments.title: The merger of the Black and white musicians' unions
segments.summary: The merged 802 opened downtown hotel jobs to Black musicians that white contractors had controlled.

segments.chapter: Depression gigs, Lil Armstrong, joining Chick Webb
segments.title: Gigging with Elmer Snowden and other contractors
segments.summary: After the Club Kentucky McRae worked jobs for contractors like Elmer Snowden, who ran several bands in hotels and on Long Island on the same night.

segments.chapter: Depression gigs, Lil Armstrong, joining Chick Webb
segments.title: Hanging out with Chick Webb before the Savoy job
segments.summary: Chick, still forming his band, told McRae he would be his next tenor man; they ate fifteen-cent Southern dinners on Lenox Avenue.

segments.chapter: Depression gigs, Lil Armstrong, joining Chick Webb
segments.title: Club job in Albany, New York
segments.summary: Booking agent Charlie Green sent McRae to a gangster-run club in Albany to join a clarinetist from Philadelphia.

segments.chapter: Depression gigs, Lil Armstrong, joining Chick Webb
segments.title: Stuff Smith's band and Charlie Green's plan for Lil Armstrong
segments.summary: McRae had worked with Stuff Smith in 1935; Green bought Smith's band for Lil Armstrong while Louis Armstrong was in Europe.

segments.chapter: Depression gigs, Lil Armstrong, joining Chick Webb
segments.title: Lil Armstrong's band at the Vendome Hotel in Buffalo
segments.summary: McRae joined Lil Armstrong's band in Buffalo, where he met the Will Mastin Trio, then played the Harlem Theater in New York.

segments.chapter: Depression gigs, Lil Armstrong, joining Chick Webb
segments.title: Lil Armstrong's Midwest tour and breakup
segments.summary: Green booked the band across the Midwest and Kentucky; it disbanded in Lexington and Lil went to New York.

segments.chapter: Depression gigs, Lil Armstrong, joining Chick Webb
segments.title: Chick Webb asks McRae to join on the road
segments.summary: Back in New York, Bardu Ali relays Chick's request; McRae leaves the next morning with thirty-six dollars borrowed from Chick's band to travel.

segments.chapter: Depression gigs, Lil Armstrong, joining Chick Webb
segments.title: Months of travel with Chick Webb's band
segments.summary: They toured south to Florida, then back through Cincinnati, Chicago and out west for six months straight.

segments.chapter: Depression gigs, Lil Armstrong, joining Chick Webb
segments.title: Kansas City jam session and Charlie Parker
segments.summary: On the road to Kansas City the overloaded bus was swapped; at the Subway Club jam session set up for Chick, they first saw Charlie Parker, who rode with the band.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Jam sessions at the Rhythm Club
segments.summary: Welburn steers back to 1932-36; McRae says the Rhythm Club was where musicians jammed, usually at night.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Day jobs musicians held
segments.summary: Few musicians had day jobs; those who did worked in stores or elevators, while many lived off gigs.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Scarcity of recording and the rise of ballrooms
segments.summary: Little recording went on before the big-band cycle, which moved bands from night clubs into ballrooms and society clubs.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Recording with Benny Morton and Jerry Blake
segments.summary: Welburn lists McRae's early 1934 sessions with Benny Morton and asks about Jerry Blake, who McRae knew from hotel gigs.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: How recording dates and society gigs were staffed
segments.summary: Leaders like Red Allen or Teddy Wilson picked particular players for each date, so personnels changed from session to session.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Musicians as gentlemen
segments.summary: McRae recalls musicians as dignified, well-dressed men, such as Coleman Hawkins strolling on 7th Avenue.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Stable bands: Don Redman, Fletcher Henderson, Chick Webb broadcasts
segments.summary: McRae says the great bands stayed together like families, and listeners across the country ran to the radio for Henderson and Webb.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: The clean life of band musicians
segments.summary: The pay was modest but the life was clean; players in top bands had to live like gentlemen, with little drug use.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Duke Ellington's hiring habits
segments.summary: Ellington brought only outstanding men into the band and never changed the sound without reason.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Duke Ellington's interest in McRae and bass sax
segments.summary: Duke wanted McRae for bass clarinet or bass sax, but he stayed with Chick; Ellington remembered what he heard and prized Mary Lou Williams.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Ben Webster, the bad boy of Duke's band
segments.summary: McRae tells how Webster stumbled into the pit at the Jump for Joy rehearsal and walked away from arguments at a Minton's gathering of tenor men.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Decline of the big bands
segments.summary: McRae says the big bands began to lose the crowds as promoters oversold, the Depression bit and musicians tired of travel.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Putney Dandridge recording dates and getting paid
segments.summary: McRae explains that studio dates were one-off jobs, paid at the union, whose records were sometimes released in Europe first.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: The June 1936 independent dates with Cozy Cole and John Kirby
segments.summary: Welburn lists June 1, 1936 titles with Bobby Stark, Cozy, John Kirby and Teddy Wilson, which McRae remembers as independent dates.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Teddy Wilson sessions with Billie Holiday
segments.summary: Welburn reads the personnel of the January 1936 Teddy Wilson session with Billie Holiday and a March date.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Frankie Newton
segments.summary: McRae recalls trumpeter Frankie Newton, who died young, and Rudy Powell from the 14th Street band.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: A Commodore-issued date with Ella Fitzgerald
segments.summary: The listing names Eddie Stanfield on bass and Ella on vocals; McRae never heard the record and notes that Commodore issued many such sides.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: First recording with Ella Fitzgerald on a Teddy Wilson date
segments.summary: McRae had just met Ella, not yet in Webb's band, when they cut "My Melancholy Baby" and "All My Life".

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: How Ella Fitzgerald came into Chick Webb's band
segments.summary: Chick picked Ella from the Apollo amateur show while McRae was away with Lil Armstrong; she was in the band six months before him.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: How studio dates were staffed and run in one take
segments.summary: Leaders hand-picked reliable men; they tuned up, ran each tune down once and recorded a single take, often without music.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Red Allen's Vocalion dates and sidemen
segments.summary: Red Allen's sessions used no written music; Welburn lists titles and sidemen like Pete Clark, Clyde Hart, Tab Smith and Cozy Cole.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Head arrangements in the studio, never any music
segments.summary: McRae insists he never saw sheet music on these dates; the players worked out introductions and backgrounds on the spot.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Head-arranged "Broadway" with Dakota Staton
segments.summary: On a Late Late Show date, McRae and a team of top players put together "Broadway" for Dakota Staton without any written arrangement.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Records cut in New York but released in Europe first
segments.summary: Charlie Johnson's RCA sides were cut on 23rd Street; companies often issued jazz in Europe first because of the strong market.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Coleman Hawkins's "Body and Soul" and selling it in Boston
segments.summary: McRae recalls Hawkins's letter and buys 500 copies for Harvard students while Hawkins was in Europe; Welburn corrects the dating.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Mother's Lunch, the Boston boarding house and chicken place
segments.summary: McRae describes living on the top floor above Mother's Lunch, where Artie Shaw's men came to eat chicken and play records.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Studio session length and ease of cutting four sides
segments.summary: Sessions ran about three hours and top musicians could do four sides easily.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Why leaders assembled special all-star players for dates
segments.summary: Teddy Wilson or Red Allen picked players for the sound they wanted rather than the men in their working bands.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Decca's poor sound versus RCA's Erskine Hawkins records
segments.summary: McRae fought with Decca over a bad-sounding Ella date after hearing Erskine Hawkins's "Tuxedo Junction" on RCA.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Start of Tape 3, studios compared
segments.summary: Tape 3 begins; McRae continues comparing Decca and Brunswick studios with RCA's 23rd Street studio.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Louis Armstrong's "Sit Down, You're Rockin' the Boat" date
segments.summary: McRae helped engineer an Armstrong date where the Sy Oliver arrangements had not been delivered, and they discuss Armstrong's schooling.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: The Decca "Where is the melody" sign and Chick Webb's drums
segments.summary: Decca's studio was cramped, with a sign asking for the melody that was covered whenever Webb's band recorded.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: RCA's 23rd Street studio
segments.summary: McRae describes the padded, high-ceilinged RCA studio, where Fats Waller and many others recorded.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Studio pianos: Steinway, Baldwin and Art Tatum's tuning
segments.summary: Steinway serviced the studios, pianos were kept at 440, and a tuner came every other day for Art Tatum.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Getting copies of one's records
segments.summary: Musicians bought copies or got one from the leader; records were a side thing next to live performance.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Calling the same top men; first-take dates
segments.summary: Leaders used reliable players like Cozy Cole, and McRae recalls running down keys and introductions and recording first takes.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Playing head arrangements with his own band, "Mr. Bear"
segments.summary: On a 1956 tour his band's best numbers were head arrangements that puzzled a rival band wanting to see the charts.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Chick Webb's collective head arrangements and Prez on dates
segments.summary: The Webb band's "Tiger Rag" and blues were built by the men together; the same went for Duke and for Billie Holiday and Lester Young dates.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Whether McRae led bands of his own
segments.summary: He says the McRae Brothers was his only early band and that he led big bands in 1945-47.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Gig pay and where club dates were played
segments.summary: Gigs paid twenty-five to forty dollars a night; they discuss hotels, weddings and New Jersey weekend dates.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Brooklyn work, Austin Powell and Louis Jordan, and the Club Sudan
segments.summary: Questions about Brooklyn lead to McRae's 1945 Town Hill job, Austin Powell's return and his rock-and-roll writing.

segments.chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
segments.title: Brothers Dave and Bob; Schillinger method
segments.summary: After the Club Kentucky closed, McRae played with brother Dave in White Plains; Bob studied at Juilliard, prompting talk of the Schillinger system.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Chick Webb's move to broaden the band; McRae as straw boss
segments.summary: After the road trip the band had money from one-nighters and McRae took over details for Webb, picking music for Ella.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Jack Robbins's music-publishing deal
segments.summary: Publisher Jack Robbins offered free arrangements and early hit songs for a weekly coast-to-coast Savoy broadcast.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Going commercial; John Hammond; the Casa Loma sound
segments.summary: McRae tells Hammond to stay quiet about the band's change toward pop, and recalls Glen Gray finding his sound.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Publisher songs, new arrangers, and more time for Ella
segments.summary: Shapiro-Bernstein and Mills also supplied songs; McRae hired Jimmy Mundy and Van Alexander and gave Ella more broadcast time.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Ella borrowed for Benny Goodman's Camel show
segments.summary: Goodman wanted Ella for the Robbins hit "Please Be Kind" on his radio show, naming the singers who preceded Helen Forrest.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: "A-Tisket, A-Tasket" makes Ella a feature attraction
segments.summary: Ella was built into a featured act, and "A-Tisket, A-Tasket" gave her a hit.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Ella arriving in Savannah after a day on the bus
segments.summary: Ella had to dress on the bus before greeting crowds of girls; one-nighters were especially hard on a woman traveling.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Bardu Ali, the front man of Chick's band
segments.summary: Bardu Ali fronted the band as a showman and dancer; later Babe Wallace fronted it before Benny Carter declined to take over.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Replacing Elmer Williams in Chick Webb's saxes
segments.summary: Elmer Williams would not travel, and Chick had promised McRae the job; the band was house band at the Savoy.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Band personnel on McRae's arrival: brass and reeds
segments.summary: Welburn and McRae go through trumpets, trombones (Nat Story, Sandy Williams) and the reed section including Wayman Carver.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Don Kirkpatrick and Tommy Fulford
segments.summary: Kirkpatrick was a fine arranger who stayed home when the band travelled, replaced by Tommy Fulford in late 1936.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Louis Jordan in the reed section
segments.summary: Jordan came in as Carver left for Atlanta; he played second alto and baritone while Pete Clark led.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Chick Webb's Little Chicks; Van Alexander
segments.summary: Webb and Cab Calloway formed small units; McRae identifies arranger Van Alexander.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Ella Fitzgerald's Savoy Eight and later reed changes
segments.summary: Welburn lists November 1936 Savoy Eight sides and the changes: Haughton, Garvin Bushell, Hilton Jefferson.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Beverly Peer and the Webb band's recorded history
segments.summary: They cover bassist Beverly Peer and the sidemen on Webb recordings from 1933 on, including Charles Linton's vocals.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Back at the Savoy: broadcasts and college dates
segments.summary: After the road trip the band broadcast from the Savoy and played holiday dates at Yale and Harvard.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Boston engagement at La Vodges with Artie Shaw's band
segments.summary: Chick's band broke records at a Boston eatery while Artie Shaw's band played nearby, where McRae started writing for Shaw.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Writing "Traffic Jam" for Artie Shaw
segments.summary: Shaw pressed McRae for a closing theme and McRae stalled with eight bars, which became "Traffic Jam".

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Commuting from Boston on the 12:05 train
segments.summary: Musicians worked in Boston but returned to New York each weekend.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Chick Webb's declining health
segments.summary: Webb's back trouble worsened; fluid was drained and Big Sid Catlett and Bill Beeson subbed on the drums.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Chick Webb's last talk at Keyes Restaurant
segments.summary: On the final trip, Webb asked McRae to take care of the band and Ella.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Playing Montgomery without knowing Webb had died
segments.summary: The band played sets for a silent crowd until the manager told them Webb had died that afternoon.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Webb's trip back to Baltimore and his family
segments.summary: McRae recounts Webb driving home for his operation and answers Welburn's questions about his wife, sister and pictures.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Tape 4: new session, Catherine Golter present
segments.summary: A second session on October 8, 1981, opens with an apprentice interviewer present, and the interviewers return to Webb's death.

segments.chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
segments.title: Chick Webb's wake and funeral in Baltimore
segments.summary: The band attends the wake in Webb's Baltimore home, where thousands filed through.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: Bill Beeson takes Chick's drum chair
segments.summary: The band returns to the Savoy briefly; senior men run it, with Chick's friend Bill Beeson on drums, though no one could fill Chick's place.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: Resetting the book without Chick Webb
segments.summary: The week at the Savoy was spent cutting drum solos and reworking the opening numbers; Ella stayed the star as the band rebuilt.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: The Savoy battle with Benny Goodman
segments.summary: A tall substitute drummer broke up the house on "By Heck", then Chick sat in for "King Porter Stomp" to open the battle, after the band changed tempos to fool Goodman.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: "Goodnight My Love" and Ella on Goodman's Camel show
segments.summary: Jack Robbins gave the band the hit first; Ella sight-read arrangements quickly, and Goodman borrowed her and the arrangement for his broadcast.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: Writing "You Showed Me the Way" with Bud Green
segments.summary: Robbins paired McRae's melody with lyricist Bud Green; credit was shared with Ella and Chick Webb.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: McRae's staff-writer contract with Robbins Music
segments.summary: The Robbins deal was an advance against royalties of a thousand dollars, rising to five and ten thousand yearly.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: Royalties and writing "Back Bay Shuffle" for Artie Shaw
segments.summary: The song sold well abroad; Shaw and McRae both signed with Robbins and agreed to split credit on songs written for him.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: Writing "Moon Ray" with Artie Shaw at the Brickwood
segments.summary: McRae recalls Shaw hanging out in Harlem and the bass part he gave him for a theme; he praises Shaw as arranger and clarinetist.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: "Traffic Jam" with Chick, and Chick buying arrangements
segments.summary: The Shaw tunes were redone for Chick; Webb spent his last dime on arrangements by Henderson, Charlie Dixon and Jimmy Mundy.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: How McRae came to lead the band after Webb's death
segments.summary: The band played Chicago and New York dates, and when Benny Carter wanted Ella as his own, Moe Gale gave the band to McRae.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: A week at Loew's State and unkind reviews
segments.summary: The band played Loew's State; critics said Beeson looked like the ghost of Chick Webb.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: Ella hands over the baton; Elmer Williams rejoins
segments.summary: In Chicago, Ella told McRae to lead the band, Babe Wallace had disappeared, and Elmer Williams borrowed a tenor from Coleman Hawkins.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: Jesse Price replaces Bill Beeson
segments.summary: After a bus quarrel with Ella, Moe Gale's office hired Kansas City drummer Jesse Price, a near copy of Chick, who joined for the western tour.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: Los Angeles: record crowds and Ella's film
segments.summary: The band broke attendance records out west while Ella made a Hollywood picture; four big bands were in town.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: Waltzes and tangos at the Trianon Ballroom
segments.summary: Western dancers wanted waltzes, so the band played pop waltzes and authentic tangos with arrangements from Sampson and Dr. Steel.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: The band as a family; Bobby Stark
segments.summary: McRae explains rehearsals as corrections among equals, including trumpeter Bobby Stark, whose solos other bands imitated.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: Playing tangos properly; Chick Webb the self-made drummer
segments.summary: Webb insisted on correct tempos and slow rolls; McRae describes his self-made drive and ambition.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: Publishers' night and song pluggers at rehearsal
segments.summary: Song pluggers attended a weekly rehearsal and left copies; McRae and Ella later went through the songs privately to choose.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: Reviving back-of-the-book arrangements
segments.summary: Rehearsed arrangements stored in the book were pulled out when the band's spirit was high.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: Tommy Fulford, Ram Ramirez and Lonnie Simmons
segments.summary: Fulford fell ill and died; Ramirez filled in; McRae hired Lonnie Simmons, who later led a combo in Chicago.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: West Coast tour: Sweet's ballrooms, Portland key to the city
segments.summary: After the Trianon the band played Oakland, Seattle and Portland, met Fats Waller, and Ella gave a moving medley.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: Duke Ellington's "Jump for Joy" in Los Angeles
segments.summary: McRae praises Duke's show, took Ella to see it, and recalls Ben Webster stumbling into the pit.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: Chicago union welcomes McRae
segments.summary: Returning east through Chicago, the Black local's officers and some fifty members came to greet him.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: Coleman Hawkins's horn, and Lonnie Simmons joins
segments.summary: Elmer kept Hawkins's tenor and McRae bought him another; Lonnie Simmons then played the Famous Door, Roseland and Apollo.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: Boston hotel engagement and the dispute with Moe Gale
segments.summary: A "Dizzy" filled the tenor chair for four weeks in Boston; McRae pressed Moe Gale for more pay and a share, but Gale reneged.

segments.chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
segments.title: Leaving Ella's band after the Holyoke meeting
segments.summary: At a meeting with Gale, Ella and Eddie Barefield, McRae walked out over the unsigned agreement and left that night, without bitterness.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Why McRae never joined Duke: pay compared with other bands
segments.summary: He says Duke paid too little compared with white-band tenor men, and says Lionel Hampton later paid him top salary.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Travelling by bus with Chick Webb
segments.summary: The band travelled in one bus, overloaded with baggage, and played big dates like the twelve thousand crowd in Kansas City.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: The fallen money bag prank
segments.summary: McRae hid one of the bags at the Kansas City gate count to tease Chick and the Gales.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Buses, drivers and the route through the states
segments.summary: Moe Gale rented a Greyhound-type bus; they played all the main towns on the way west.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Staying in private homes and small hotels
segments.summary: On tour the band often stayed with local people because hotels were small or segregated.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: No trouble on the road; the Greenville private club
segments.summary: McRae says bands were welcomed everywhere; they played a private casino club in Greenville, Mississippi.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Overcharging the band at restaurants and hotels
segments.summary: Restaurants removed menus and a Birmingham hotel charged five dollars a night to a band, which led to the next story.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: The band's trick to rent a hotel cheaply
segments.summary: The musicians parked the bus away and checked in a few at a time, renting the whole hotel before the owner knew.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Muslim band members posing as African diplomats
segments.summary: On tour with Louis Armstrong, two sidemen in turbans got hotel rooms as diplomats until their uniforms gave them away.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Edgar Sampson's arrangements for Webb
segments.summary: Welburn asks about arrangements; McRae recalls gigging with Chick in 1933-34 and Chick's habit of buying arrangements.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Chick's library and Sampson's tunes in the book
segments.summary: On joining the band McRae found enough music for two books, with Henderson charts and Sampson arrangements.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Becoming music director; putting "Stompin' at the Savoy" forward
segments.summary: McRae went through the book and pushed "Stompin' at the Savoy", which then went over big.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Benny Goodman hears the band; Fletcher Henderson on the road
segments.summary: Goodman, Shaw and others watched Webb's band on Saturday nights; Chick's band avoided Fletcher's best-known numbers when they met on the road.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: McRae's dual tenor role and the band improving
segments.summary: He played both sweet and hot tenor parts, wrote backgrounds for Ella and kept pressing Chick to play new numbers.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Three-way credit for "Stompin' at the Savoy"
segments.summary: McRae persuaded Sampson to give Goodman a third of the song, so Goodman's Camel show would make it a hit.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: How the Goodman exposure helped Webb and Sampson
segments.summary: Goodman recorded "Blue Lou" and "Don't Be That Way", boosting Webb's book and leading to the battle.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Why Edgar Sampson left the band
segments.summary: Sampson quit after a fight at a Maryland dance because he would not travel South.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Hiring Louis Jordan
segments.summary: Jordan was hired on third alto and baritone and was well liked.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: "Frost on the Moon" feature for Ella, Jordan and Linton
segments.summary: They created a vocal trio feature for the Apollo and discussed how each singer's feature was planned.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Planning Louis Jordan's role so it never overshadowed Ella
segments.summary: Everything Jordan did was agreed beforehand, since he had to fit the band like a puzzle and not compete with Ella.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Ella's songs and Robbins's Hollywood tunes
segments.summary: Ella made every song her own; the band stayed ahead by getting top Hollywood songs, and Chick saw her talent early.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Songs selected for Ella from Rust's discography
segments.summary: Welburn reads titles like "Spring Fever Blues" and McRae confirms they were chosen for her.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: "Mr. Paganini" and novelty numbers for Ella
segments.summary: A novelty by a husband-and-wife team shows how Ella could handle any style, with songs sprung on her only when ready.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: How Ella learned new songs
segments.summary: Ella heard the arrangement run down, took lyric cards home, and returned having memorized them; many songs were turned down.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: "A-Tisket, A-Tasket" as Ella's own idea; hiring Van Alexander
segments.summary: The song was Ella's nursery-rhyme number; Van Alexander, hired as pop arranger, wrote it down.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Arrangers' rehearsal schedule at the Boston engagement
segments.summary: Arrangers like Van, Mundy and Dixon came on set days; special rehearsals were held for Ella apart from big-band rehearsals.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: How McRae gained responsibility; Chick wanted a hot and smooth tenor
segments.summary: After the first tour McRae took on duties; Chick wanted his Herschel Evans-like style after Elmer Williams.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Cleaning up the band section by section
segments.summary: McRae and Taft Jordan began rehearsals to tighten the sections; a leader assigns solos to who can play them and knows the men.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Why Shaw's Boston band could not play "Traffic Jam"
segments.summary: Shaw's band could not handle it, so he rebuilt his band before recording the hit version.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Building a new band for Louis Armstrong under Joe Glaser
segments.summary: Glaser sent McRae to hear Armstrong's old band in Roanoke; later McRae replaced a drinking brass section.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Army and Navy base shows as Armstrong's music director
segments.summary: Airlifted to bases for two concerts a day, the band played a secret B-29 plant in Arizona without leaving the vehicle.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: The music director's duties with Armstrong; the film "Pillar to Post"
segments.summary: McRae handled broadcasts, arrangements and rehearsals for Armstrong, who wanted no responsibility, including a MGM soundtrack.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: The Zanzibar and Roxy show with Bill Robinson
segments.summary: Glaser tested McRae with the Zanzibar show, which he rehearsed with Bill Robinson's act in Washington and doubled with the Roxy.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Uniforms, road managers and valets
segments.summary: McRae lists the road manager and valets, buying suits at Young and Taylor, and the clothes changes with Chick versus Cab Calloway.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Transcription work in New York
segments.summary: Chick's band made radio transcriptions that stopped without explanation as hotels piped in softer music.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: RCA-NBC broadcast recordings and Decca versus RCA sound
segments.summary: Welburn lists Webb's January 1939 RCA radio sides; McRae returns to his complaint about Decca's sound and Milt Gabler.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Webb's battles with Goodman, Casa Loma and Duke
segments.summary: McRae thinks the Goodman battle was overblown; Webb outplayed Casa Loma with "Hold That Tiger" and respected Duke's band.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: The Chick Webb versus Duke Ellington battle at the Savoy
segments.summary: Webb made Duke's band work; Duke answered with "Big John Special", and the floor shook.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Reed section structure and the "million dollar reed section"
segments.summary: McRae lays out chair assignments, then recalls the Saturday-afternoon reed rehearsals above Manny's on 48th Street.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Tuning, matching vibrato and breathing together
segments.summary: The reed men matched tone and vibrato to the lead player and marked where to breathe, so phrases sounded as one.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
