segments.title: Mutes, matching sounds, and Stan Kenton's Ellington imitation
segments.summary: Brass sections cut mute corks to match; Kenton tried for Ellington's sound but Duke's plunger effects confused white musicians.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Duke's voicings, and arrangers who know the instruments
segments.summary: Duke and Strayhorn built unusual chords, and Benny Carter wrote saxophone parts that lay perfectly.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Arranging behind singers and soloists without overwriting
segments.summary: Good arrangers write to help the singer, and overwritten band parts can drown a soloist.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Chick's tempo-shift break at the Goodman battle
segments.summary: Webb's break shifted into waltz time against a fast four, leaving McRae and Vido Musso lost on their entry.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Arrangers who overwrite, and Chick tearing up charts
segments.summary: Some charts were torn up when they did not work; Chick preferred keeping them in the book.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Chauncey Haughton and Pete Clark in the alto chairs
segments.summary: Haughton led the reed section as concertmaster, Clark played third alto and clarinet solos.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Dressing on the bus and playing two sets without the books
segments.summary: The band changed on the bus, valets set up the stand, and head arrangements like "St. Louis Blues" opened sets.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Chick Webb's back and the New York operation
segments.summary: Welburn asks whether Webb's affliction hampered his drumming; McRae recalls his Baltimore fall and the operation he thought hurt him.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Strain at the Paramount, a late Decca session and the final illness
segments.summary: Joe Saunders carried the exhausted Webb offstage between Paramount shows; they recorded "Spanish Tour" at night, then Webb went to Hopkins.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: The band's shock in Baltimore and Ella following McRae
segments.summary: After the Montgomery news, the shock hit in Baltimore, where Ella followed McRae through the streets crying.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: The funeral at Waters AME Church and Ella's song
segments.summary: McRae thinks he played "My Buddy" on tenor at the service and hopes to get Baltimore newspaper photographs.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Chick Webb's drum equipment: tympani heads, sticks, cymbals
segments.summary: Webb used xylophone and tympani, tympani heads on his drums, carefully chosen sticks and Zildjian cymbals, and pioneered the hi-hat.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Chick Webb did not read music; his drive and followers
segments.summary: McRae says Webb had feeling and ideas, and that Charlie Persip and others idolized him.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Chick brings young Buddy Rich to sit in
segments.summary: Webb let Buddy Rich play a set at the Savoy and told the band to remember his name.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Cozy Cole, a learned drummer
segments.summary: McRae calls Cozy a master who played with philharmonic orchestras.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Cozy Cole and Milt Hinton in Cab Calloway's band
segments.summary: Drummers visited Cozy between shows; McRae shared a dressing room with Hinton and listened to classical records.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Whether Black musicians could read music
segments.summary: McRae objects to the idea that Black musicians could not read, citing Armstrong, Jabbo Smith and Jenkins Orphanage graduates.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Why McRae switched from Conn to Selmer saxophone
segments.summary: Welburn asks about the switch; McRae says the Conn was too weak to be heard across the packed Savoy.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Trading in the Conn at Manny's and trying the Selmer
segments.summary: He got a Selmer and Otto Link mouthpiece; the new horn sounded distant until he got used to it.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Ben Webster tries McRae's Selmer
segments.summary: Webster blew McRae's horn at the Paramount and immediately bought one at Manny's, starting a switch from Conn to Selmer.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: The Selmer's carrying power at the Kansas City auditorium and Savoy
segments.summary: McRae recalls not being heard in a crowd of 12,000 with the Conn and being heard clearly with the Selmer.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Conn bass sax and rubber mouthpieces
segments.summary: He liked the Conn bass sax, rarely used baritone, and used rubber mouthpieces before the Link caught on.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Reeds and how he shaved them
segments.summary: McRae used strength four and a half or five, shaved the length, and favored King reeds.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Carrying reeds on the road; Vido Musso takes the sixes
segments.summary: He travelled with several boxes of reeds, and Vido Musso walked off with three boxes of number sixes.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Heat on the road and caring for horns
segments.summary: In Texas and Oklahoma heat the reeds cracked; they used wet towels, oiled pads, and later enjoyed the Selmer's built-in springs.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Cleaning and repairing horns on tour
segments.summary: The musicians cleaned their own horns nightly and had a repairman restore a horn after a trunk was dropped on it.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: The Link mouthpiece for tenor soloists
segments.summary: Tenor men used Link mouthpieces to cut above the brass, while altos mostly stayed with rubber ones.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Never going back from the Selmer; borrowing and renting horns
segments.summary: McRae never played anything else after the Selmer, and a name band member could borrow or rent a horn easily.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Coleman Hawkins and the Selmer advertisements
segments.summary: Selmer's pictures of Hawkins with a gold Selmer drove McRae and many tenor players to switch; Hawkins visited the Savoy.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: Chick Webb in ads; hi-hat, tempo blocks and the "run around"
segments.summary: Webb appeared in drum ads and McRae describes his use of hi-hat and tempo blocks.

segments.chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
segments.title: The first night with the Selmer
segments.summary: McRae sweated through a set because he could not hear the new horn, but the sound carried out front.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Songwriting for Robbins after Boston
segments.summary: McRae stayed in New York writing for the Robbins staff, including "Santa Rosa" and "I'm Afraid of Love".

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Sheet music for "Love, Love, Love", "Santa Rosa" and "You Showed Me the Way"
segments.summary: Welburn reads credits and recordings for McRae's published songs, including the Clovers and Diamonds versions.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Choosing a song's key; song pluggers and sheet music
segments.summary: Songs are published in the key that fits the average singer, and five-and-ten song demonstrators played them in any key.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: After leaving Ella: Glaser's offer and the Chick Webb memorial concert plan
segments.summary: McRae planned a memorial concert with Moe Gale's backing and star drummers, while considering a move to Joe Glaser.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Chick's sister and the money held by Moe Gale
segments.summary: McRae told Chick's sister to ask the Moe Gale office for money Chick had banked there, which angered Gale.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Sally Webb and copyright renewals through John Eastman
segments.summary: McRae put Chick Webb's widow in touch with lawyer John Eastman, who paid for the renewals of Chick's copyrights.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Why the memorial concert never happened
segments.summary: Gale took a trip abroad and died soon after; Norman Granz agreed to lend Ella but the project lapsed.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Cab Calloway calls after Chu Berry's accident
segments.summary: Cab's manager found McRae on Broadway and sent him to Toronto and Montreal, where he learned Berry had died.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Joining Cab Calloway for ten weeks of theaters
segments.summary: McRae reluctantly agreed to help Cab out, and travelled in cold Canadian weather.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Cab's band lacked Chick's spirit
segments.summary: The band was well drilled but Cab was a showman, so McRae told the men he came from the big tent.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Rehearsing Cab's reeds and rebuilding the band
segments.summary: Working with Hilton Jefferson-era sidemen, McRae called section rehearsals and Cab's sections began to play better.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: The Strand Theater success and the Cab Drivers "Nature Boy" arrangement
segments.summary: Reviewers called the Strand engagement Cab's best-sounding band; McRae wrote a chant ending and small-band numbers.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Using idle weeks in the theater to rehearse
segments.summary: During five weeks in the theater McRae and Jeff rehearsed the book and the other sections joined.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: The Palmer Brothers and Cab's recordings
segments.summary: McRae describes the Palmer Brothers vocal group and Cab's records "I'll Be Around" and "Minnie the Moocher".

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: The Cabaliers and records made in Chicago
segments.summary: Welburn asks about the Cabaliers; McRae recalls recording "Minnie the Moocher" and "I'll Be Around" in Chicago.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Leaving Cab Calloway before the California trip
segments.summary: McRae left Cab at the Chicago Theater rather than go away from his children; Welburn lists the reed section in Hollywood.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Replacements: Al Gibson and Sam "The Man" Taylor
segments.summary: McRae recommended Al Gibson and later woke Sam "The Man" Taylor to get him a job with Cab.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Called by Lunceford while John Hammond wanted him at NBC
segments.summary: A wire reached McRae to replace Joe Thomas for two months in Akron, though Hammond had offered an NBC staff job.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Preparing to replace Joe Thomas; the Lunceford drummer's bet
segments.summary: McRae learned the Lunceford records beforehand, played the hard book and "Let's Keep Smiling", and won the drummer's bet.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Lunceford's books left on the train
segments.summary: The band played the whole Washington show from memory after the music books stayed on the baggage car.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Lunceford's alto and sax section: Willie Smith and Hilton Jefferson
segments.summary: McRae rates Willie Smith, Chauncey Haughton and Hilton Jefferson against Johnny Hodges and Benny Carter.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Earl Carruthers and Harry Carney on baritone
segments.summary: McRae praises both baritone players and calls Carney a once-in-a-lifetime player and Duke's work lasting art.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Carney's classical riffs and Gunable's mouthpiece training
segments.summary: McRae recalls Carney's technical control and returns to Gunable's lessons on embouchure, saying Foots Thomas wanted to teach him.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Cat Anderson's high C's and his teacher
segments.summary: McRae says Cat Anderson's non-pressure study with a teacher let him hit five C's, which no one on television bands could match.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Trumpet players who push themselves: Freddy Webster, Shavers, Eldridge
segments.summary: Some good trumpeters never promote themselves, unlike Charlie Shavers and Roy Eldridge, who stayed in the spotlight.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Draft status, USO plans and the recording ban
segments.summary: McRae was a family man and cannot recall how he avoided the draft; his brothers went on the USO and Shaw's Navy band, and Lunceford made no records.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Famous Door with Art Tatum and the NBC Piano Playhouse
segments.summary: McRae worked three months at the Famous Door where Billie Holiday followed, and watched Art Tatum on the NBC Piano Playhouse.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Walking 52nd Street with Joe Glaser, Winchell and Ed Sullivan
segments.summary: McRae became friends with Glaser, strolling to Cafe Society with Jack Robbins, Walter Winchell and Ed Sullivan.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Glaser asks McRae to build a new band for Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: Glaser sent him to hear Armstrong's band and told him to rebuild it; Welburn lists the new personnel.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Tape 8, October 13, 1981: why McRae left Cab
segments.summary: A new session opens and Welburn asks about leaving Cab Calloway; McRae didn't want to go back to California or do studio work.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Writing rhythm and blues for publishers
segments.summary: With Sid Wyche, Charlie Singleton and others, McRae composed and arranged songs that publishers placed with artists.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Artie Shaw gives up his band; unrecorded tunes
segments.summary: Robbins told McRae he lost half a million dollars when Shaw quit, leaving unrecorded McRae tunes.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Les Brown arrangement and first stint with Lionel Hampton
segments.summary: A lost arrangement for Les Brown; Glaser sent McRae to Boston for two weeks with Hampton, and Dexter Gordon's departure kept him on.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Moving from big bands to R&B
segments.summary: McRae explains he didn't want to take other musicians' club jobs, so he gigged, recorded and wrote.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Writing "Love, Love, Love" with Sid Wyche; BMI pen names
segments.summary: With Wyche he wrote his first rock-and-roll hit, publishing under pseudonyms Thomas Bear and William Gray for BMI.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Why he left the road: the kids and Cab's California trip
segments.summary: McRae joined ASCAP in 1945 and left Cab to be home, since touring meant eighteen weeks of theaters.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Who replaced McRae in Cab's band
segments.summary: Al Gibson replaced him, and Cab later asked for another tenor, so McRae got Sam "The Man" Taylor.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: "Run Joe" Taylor and "The Great Pretender"
segments.summary: McRae names co-writers and recalls that Taylor sold "The Great Pretender" for fifty dollars before it became the Platters' hit.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Writing with Una Mae Carlisle
segments.summary: McRae recalls working weeks on each song with pianist Una Mae Carlisle, who wrote "Walking by the River"; Welburn adds her death in 1956.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Writing for King Records: Henry Glover and Dossie Terry
segments.summary: With Charlie Singleton and Glover, McRae wrote songs for Wynonie Harris and the "Thunderbird" jingle.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: How McRae came to replace Joe Thomas in Lunceford's band
segments.summary: Lunceford's tenor Joe Thomas wanted time off, and Lunceford had tried several tenor players who couldn't play his hard book.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Lunceford's difficult saxophone book
segments.summary: McRae studied "Walking by the River" and its double-time sax chorus, expecting his Chick Webb background to carry him.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Learning another man's solos without imitating him
segments.summary: McRae learned the Joe Thomas feature but played around it, a method he also used with Hawkins patterns.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Learning parts from records
segments.summary: He learned the saxophone parts by listening to records, reading well and following the lead alto.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Following a strong lead alto and reading ahead
segments.summary: A second tenor follows the lead alto and chord pattern, reading a bar or two ahead rather than note for note.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Sitting in for Coleman Hawkins in Fletcher Henderson's band
segments.summary: His wife called McRae to replace Hawkins one night at the Roseland, where they pulled out the hardest book he had seen.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Meeting his own "Body and Soul" arrangement in Lunceford's book
segments.summary: A Pittsburgh arranger had written "Body and Soul" for McRae, sold it to Lunceford's Joe Thomas, and McRae played his own intro the first night.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: "Let's Keep Smiling" and Lunceford's trust
segments.summary: Two nights later McRae played Joe Thomas's feature too; Lunceford never doubted a man's ability.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Why New York musicians outplayed those in other cities
segments.summary: Detroit and Cleveland players couldn't read Lunceford's book; New York offered constant exposure to top players.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Territory bands, and New York's arrangers
segments.summary: Welburn notes the decline of Kansas City and territory bands; McRae says New York's arrangers like Redman and Mundy set the pace.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Lunceford's Midwest and East dates, then the Audubon
segments.summary: Over two months McRae travelled with Lunceford through the Midwest, then played the Audubon, Trenton and Washington.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Joining Lionel Hampton's band
segments.summary: McRae, who replaced Dexter Gordon, stayed with Hampton for almost three years.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: How Arnett Cobb's injury and Dexter's exit kept him with Hamp
segments.summary: After a wrestling mishap, McRae filled in; Dexter gave notice and Hamp begged him to stay rather than join Les Brown.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: The Cobb-McRae tenor team
segments.summary: Hampton called McRae and Arnett Cobb his best tenor team, who worked out showmanship routines together.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: "Lady Be Good" routine and returning to Hamp on alto
segments.summary: McRae burlesqued with Cobb and, years later, taught Lucky Thompson's section the routine when Hamp called him back.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Playing to fit the singer's mood
segments.summary: McRae says he accompanied Ella, Cab and Dinah Washington by fitting the mood, not showing off.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Artie Shaw brings Tony Pastor to hear McRae
segments.summary: Shaw sent Pastor to learn from McRae's playing, and the band greeted him at a Boston reunion.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Staying in the section: Chu Berry versus Ben Webster
segments.summary: McRae argues a soloist should keep playing his part up to his solo, as Ben Webster did, unlike Chu Berry.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Floor shows and dancers at the Savoy and on the road
segments.summary: Welburn asks about dancers; McRae describes late-night show numbers at the Savoy and road ballroom shows with Chick, Taft and Ella.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Road audiences danced more than New Yorkers
segments.summary: Road crowds danced all night since the band was there only once; the Savoy's two bands alternated set lengths.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Playing third alto for Hampton
segments.summary: McRae retrieved his alto and filled in for Hampton for a couple of months before joining Armstrong.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Building Armstrong's new band and becoming musical director
segments.summary: Joe Glaser wanted a younger band for Louis Armstrong, whose old band was losing men, and put McRae in charge.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Music director for Armstrong; the command performance joke
segments.summary: Armstrong left everything to McRae, including a command performance where he stopped the band on air, joking he wanted McRae's name broadcast.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Bill Robinson and Louis Armstrong as deep thinkers
segments.summary: McRae finds both men gentle, thoughtful behind their showman faces.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Rehearsing "Don't Fence Me In" late at night
segments.summary: Armstrong stayed late despite plans to go uptown, and the record became one of the biggest McRae worked on.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Dexter Gordon joins Armstrong; the "Grooving" session
segments.summary: The 1944 Decca sides come up; Dexter joined in California for about a month during wartime travel.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Writing Armstrong into spots rather than blowing throughout
segments.summary: McRae built a heavier band and spotted Armstrong in arrangements to rest his lip; Glaser objected until it worked in Canada.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: "Grooving" credits and R. I. O'Nan
segments.summary: McRae finished a pencil sketch by trumpeter Frank Brown and another writer; they listen to the recording.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Coca-Cola broadcasts and precise timing
segments.summary: The band did nineteen Coca-Cola shows, each timed exactly to the half hour with the producer cueing cuts through earphones.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Wartime schedule and unissued sides
segments.summary: Edgar Sampson wrote on the road while the band worked nearly every night, with Army and Navy hospital shows and transcriptions.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Dorothy Dandridge and the "Pillar to Post" soundtrack
segments.summary: Dandridge sang once with Armstrong in the film, whose trick arrangements had to be simplified in the recording studio.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Joining ASCAP and publishing through Robbins
segments.summary: Before 1945 McRae's songs sat with Robbins Music; joining ASCAP with a whole catalog let him collect back revenue.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Mistaken credit for Joe Thomas's song in a film
segments.summary: Shapiro-Bernstein thought a song used by Glenn Miller and Artie Shaw was McRae's, but it belonged to the other tenor player named Joe Thomas.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Wartime shortage of musicians and the decline of big bands
segments.summary: Many musicians joined the armed forces; McRae's brother Bob led a Navy band; travel limits and rising small bands undermined big bands.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Air bases, Fort Huachuca and secret security
segments.summary: Armed services flew the band to Arizona bases, where security kept them from seeing anything, and Jimmy Mundy wrote at Fort Huachuca.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: Playing for wounded soldiers at Walter Reed
segments.summary: McRae calls the hospital show one of the hardest dates of his life, as hundreds of amputees lined the aisle.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
segments.title: No overseas travel; Armstrong drops the big band
segments.summary: McRae never went overseas in the war; Armstrong later cut the big band for an all-star group after complaining of arrangement costs.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Gigging and recording in New York; writing for advances
segments.summary: McRae led a small band while preferring to write, collecting advances from publishers and record companies.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Booking agency and the Monday "Concert in Jam" in Newark
segments.summary: He booked stars like Dexter, Ben Webster, Miles Davis and Max Roach, drawing students on a Newark bar's off-night.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Charlie Parker and college kids waiting outside
segments.summary: Five hundred students waited outside until Parker arrived after a Birdland set, while McRae outbid Birdland on fees.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Booking Lyn Hope and moving into Latin acts at Lloyd's Manor
segments.summary: McRae brought Latin bands to Newark after Dexter Gordon nights and found strong audiences.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Discovering Joe Loco and booking Tito Puente
segments.summary: He tracked down Joe Loco at Tico Records, booked him at Newark and found large Latin crowds.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Latin radio on WLIB and Joe Loco at the Apollo
segments.summary: McRae persuaded a deejay to play Latin music and Joe Loco broke up the Apollo, while booker Teddy Powell controlled Newark.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Joe Loco leaves for Arnold Shaw's agency
segments.summary: After McRae built him up with three dates a night, Loco jumped to a new agent, and radio disc jockeys dropped his records.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Music director of the Zanzibar and his own Zanzibar Orchestra
segments.summary: After three months with Armstrong at the Zanzibar, McRae led the small dance band and tightened the floor show for owner Howard.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Zanzibar Orchestra records, Nita Bradley, and discography details
segments.summary: Welburn reads the personnel and labels for McRae's 1946 small-band records, including Pete Clark, Kenny Kersey and the Palmer Brothers.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: The Mr. Bear sessions for Groove
segments.summary: They sort out the Mr. Bear titles and the sidemen on the September and December 1955 RCA/Groove dates.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Bob Rolontz's label and Champion Jack Dupree's "Lonely Road Blues"
segments.summary: McRae recalls producing for Rolontz, taking Dupree to record "Lonely Road Blues" and Dupree's "When I Get Married".

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Writing for King Records; Henry Glover and Wynonie Harris
segments.summary: McRae begins explaining how Glover at King brought him in and mentions Earl Bostic from the Hampton band.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: The Club Sudan band with Henry Glover and Bill Doggett
segments.summary: At the Club Sudan, the old Cotton Club, McRae led a year-long band that included trumpeter Glover and organist Bill Doggett.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Sid Nathan of King and "All She Wanna Do Is Rock"
segments.summary: Glover went to King as arranger and producer, and McRae wrote the hit "All She Wanna Do Is Rock" for Wynonie Harris.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: The 1947 big band for the Negro theaters
segments.summary: McRae built a single big band for Gale, Schiffman and Glaser to play the Apollo, Howard and Uptown theaters.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Returning to Hampton on third alto
segments.summary: Glaser arranged a few months for McRae in Hampton's band with Lucky Thompson on tenor, as Welburn lists the 1948 personnel.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Hampton's changing band and the decline of big bands
segments.summary: Big bands were suffering as small bands like Louis Jordan's thrived and the whole scene was changing.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Gigging in New Jersey and Long Island clubs; Philadelphia
segments.summary: McRae played weekend shows in small white clubs and the Dew Drop, but rarely worked in Philadelphia, where people knew his brothers.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: The Apollo house band and rock and roll acts
segments.summary: The Apollo's house band could not play the new rock-and-roll groups, so Schiffman used a small house band and let acts bring their own musicians.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: McRae's big band at the Apollo for Schiffman
segments.summary: Schiffman heard McRae's band rehearsing and booked it, with Ike Quebec and Eddie "Lockjaw" Davis on tenor.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Preparing a show in the dressing room before the first performance
segments.summary: McRae insisted on finished rehearsed shows from the first performance, as he did at the Zanzibar and Roxy.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Quieting the Apollo with a ballad; Ike Quebec and Lockjaw
segments.summary: McRae played "Serenade to a Sleeping Beauty" so softly the house hushed, while Quebec and Davis played the hot tenor choruses.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Lockjaw's tone and advice against overdoing solos
segments.summary: McRae told Davis to cut down his overblowing and says Lucky Thompson lost his audience with long cadenzas.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Hampton overworking the audience
segments.summary: Hampton kept repeating choruses and McRae told him to stop before the crowd's enthusiasm died.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Coltrane and early Miles Davis versus later work
segments.summary: McRae says the early Coltrane and Miles sold best, and later experimental records lost the general public, citing his work at Record Shack.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Alan Freed and rock and roll displace big-band jazz
segments.summary: McRae says Freed's rock and roll made it hard for jazz records, and he recalls Stanley Turrentine recording "Broadway".

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Horace Parlan in June Clark's dancing school band
segments.summary: McRae remembers pianist Horace Parlan, with a crippled hand, working with him at a dancing school, though the dating is confusing.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: His eight children and keeping them out of show business
segments.summary: McRae discourages his daughters from the road, remembering Ella's difficulties as a woman travelling.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: How McRae became "Mr. Bear" and made "Walking the Blues"
segments.summary: At Glover's urging McRae worked with Jack Dupree, devising a record where he walked on a board while Dupree played blues.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: The flip side and the dubbed tape of "Walking the Blues"
segments.summary: McRae did a talking blues with Teacho Wiltshire for the other side and added rhythm by dubbing.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Sid Nathan hears the dub in Cincinnati
segments.summary: Glover sent the tape to Sid Nathan, who loved it and planned to record it in Cincinnati.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Release of "Walking the Blues" and Bob Rolontz's Groove label
segments.summary: King added a rhythm section to the tape and released it; RCA's new Groove label then invited McRae to record.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Copies of "Walking the Blues" and Chicago bassist Dixon
segments.summary: McRae says others copied the record, including a Chicago bass player; Welburn identifies him as a blues bassist.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Making the Mr. Bear sides with an all-star band for Groove
segments.summary: Rolontz needed rhythm and blues artists; McRae gathered Mickey Baker and others, who were surprised he was the artist.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Having Alan Freed's arranger sketch his dates; Mickey Baker's break
segments.summary: A rock-and-roll arranger sketched McRae's charts; guitarist Mickey Baker got a Groove date that produced the hit with Sylvia.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Dakota Staton's Capitol album: tunes McRae supplied
segments.summary: Staton recorded McRae songs including "Broadway", "You Showed Me the Way" and "Moon Ray" to finish an album in New York.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Conducting and engineering Staton's New York sessions
segments.summary: McRae took charge of the date with Hank Jones, Jonah Jones and Jimmy Cleveland, with head arrangements put together in minutes.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Recording from the middle of the studio floor
segments.summary: McRae sets balance by standing among the band instead of the control room, and cues the engineer.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Producing quickly to avoid overtime
segments.summary: Producers hired McRae because he finished dates without costly overtime.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Corrected parts and proofreading by copyists
segments.summary: McRae insists arrangers bring corrected parts, like Jimmy Mundy, and copying studios proofread everything.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Working in Capitol's editing room
segments.summary: McRae edited tapes at Capitol, including Sinatra material, and mostly wrote rather than played.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: His labels and publishing companies: Enrica, Rae-Cox
segments.summary: He owns Enrica and Rae-Cox labels and music companies, opened in 1959 at Broadway addresses.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Enrica and Rae-Cox rhythm-and-blues catalog
segments.summary: Welburn reads titles by the Symphonics, Butanes, Tony Rice, Shallows, Sunsets and Revelons; they charted.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: "Come On Honey" with McRae's tenor solo
segments.summary: They listen to a 1964 Enrica record and discuss the Sunsets' 1959 sides.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Jazz LPs by Edmund Hall, Benny Green and Linton Garner
segments.summary: The company issued three jazz albums before leasing them out.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Leasing the jazz masters, rack jobs and bootleg discovery
segments.summary: Jazz sales collapsed in the rock-and-roll era, so the masters were leased; Harry Fox then revealed a licensee had retitled songs to avoid royalties.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Budget lines, payola and the record slump
segments.summary: McRae explains budget labels like Pickwick, and the slump after the payola investigations.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Turning Rae-Cox into a gospel label
segments.summary: The company turned to gospel on Rae-Cox, with groups like the Brooklyn Skyways and Christian Harmonizers.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Gospel as steady business, and high costs of pop albums
segments.summary: McRae says gospel is a low-overhead business, while pop albums cost tens of thousands and the industry is in a slump.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Gospel recording costs and refusing outside tapes
segments.summary: McRae records his own groups, recalls refusing to release the Skyways' Savoy-made tape, and prefers to record artists himself.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Engineering gospel recordings himself
segments.summary: He engineers his own gospel sessions and praises James Cleveland's natural-sounding choir recordings.

segments.chapter: Bandleader, songwriter and record-label owner, 1946-81
segments.title: Clinton Utterbach's choir and later ministry
segments.summary: McRae calls Utterbach's choir sensational and perfectionist, and notes he is now a radio minister.

segments.chapter: Reflections and close
segments.title: Wrapping up: anything left to add
segments.summary: Welburn asks if anything was missed and McRae says they covered everything, including Art Tatum at the Famous Door.

segments.chapter: Reflections and close
segments.title: The Chick Webb years as the highlight of his career
segments.summary: McRae calls building the Webb band and Ella's rise his greatest experience, a school that prepared him for everything after.

segments.chapter: Reflections and close
segments.title: Delegation: Chick, Louis Armstrong and Ella left everything to him
segments.summary: Each leader left details to McRae, and he found that giving people departments worked best.

segments.chapter: Reflections and close
segments.title: Why the Webb band was his best training
segments.summary: He says working with Webb let him walk through other bands, thanks to earlier study and rubbing elbows with giants.

segments.chapter: Reflections and close
segments.title: The workload as music director in California
segments.summary: Welburn notes his health; McRae recalls the phone calls, broadcast changes and band problems on the Armstrong coast stay.

segments.chapter: Reflections and close
segments.title: Road managers like Frenchie
segments.summary: McRae explains the road manager handled office business and contracts, not the band, and names Frenchie on Armstrong's tour.

segments.chapter: Reflections and close
segments.title: Opening sets chosen for the town, like a circus
segments.summary: McRae explains Webb's numbered opening sets, picked for the crowd, and answers Frenchie's complaint with the circus comparison.

segments.chapter: Reflections and close
segments.title: Webb's book and the family band
segments.summary: Webb's library of Dixon, Mundy, Redman and Sampson arrangements and his careful choice of men made the band, like Duke's, a family.

segments.chapter: Reflections and close
segments.title: Basie's Kansas City band and the musicians' hotel in New York
segments.summary: Welburn asks about Herschel Evans and Lester Young; McRae recalls the hotel on 7th Avenue where musicians stayed.

segments.chapter: Reflections and close
segments.title: Closing thanks
segments.summary: Welburn thanks McRae on behalf of the Jazz Oral History Project and McRae says it was a joy.
